questions.q: Two bodies are having kinetic energies in the ratio $16: 9 .$ If they have same linear momentum, the ratio of their masses respectively is:
questions.solution:
The kinetic energy and the momentum of a moving object are related by

$K = \dfrac{{p}^{2}}{2m} . . . \left(1\right)$

Hence, the ratio of the kinetic energies of two objects having masses $m$ and $m '$ can be calculated as follows:

$\begin{cases}\dfrac{K}{{K}^{'}} & = & \dfrac{\dfrac{{p}^{2}}{2m}}{\dfrac{{p}^{2}}{2m '}} \\ & = & \dfrac{m '}{m} . . . \left(2\right)\end{cases}$

Substitute the ratio of the kinetic energies into equation (2) and simplify to obtain the ratio of their masses.

$\begin{cases} & ⇒ & \dfrac{16}{9} = \dfrac{m '}{m} \\ & ⇒ & m: m ' = 9: 16\end{cases}$

From equation $( 1 )$ and $( 2 )$, we get,
$⇒ {\omega}^{2}R = \dfrac{2g}{R}h$
$∴ h = \dfrac{{R}^{2}{\omega}^{2}}{2g}$

questions.q: The time taken by an object to slide down $45 °$ rough inclined plane is $n$ times as it takes to slide down a perfectly smooth $45 °$ incline plane. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the incline plane is:
questions.solution:
Let angle of inclination is $\theta = 45 °$.

Then, acceleration along the incline in case of smooth incline will be, ${a}_{1} = gsin\theta = \dfrac{g}{\sqrt{2}}$.

In case of rough incline, kinetic friction will act against the direction of motion. Normal force acting on the object will be $mgcos\theta$. Therefore, acceleration along the incline in case of rough incline will be,

${a}_{2} = gsin\theta - \mugcos\theta = \dfrac{g}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\mug}{\sqrt{2}}$.

Now as per question,

${t}_{2} = n{t}_{1}$

and as the displacement covered is the same in both case, $0 + \dfrac{1}{2}{a}_{1}{t}_{1}^{2} = 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}{a}_{2}{t}_{2}^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{g}{\sqrt{2}}{t}_{1}^{2} = \left(\dfrac{g}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\mug}{\sqrt{2}}\right){n}^{2}{t}_{1}^{2}$

$⇒ \mu = 1 - \dfrac{1}{{n}^{2}}$

questions.q: An expression of energy density is given by $u = \dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}sin\left(\dfrac{\alphax}{kt}\right)$, where $\alpha, \beta$ are constants, $x$ is displacement, $k$ is Boltzmann constant and $t$ is the temperature. The dimensions of $\beta$ will be
questions.solution:
Given that energy density $U = \dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}sin\dfrac{\alphax}{kt}$

As $\dfrac{\alphax}{kt}$ should be dimensionless, the dimensions of $\alphax$ and $kt$ should be same.

$⇒ \left[\alpha\right]\left[x\right] = \left[k\right]\left[t\right] ⇒ \left[\alpha\right] = \dfrac{\left[k\right]\left[t\right]}{\left[x\right]}$

Now,

$\left[U\right] = \dfrac{\left[\alpha\right]}{\left[\beta\right]}$

$⇒ \left[\beta\right] = \dfrac{\left[\alpha\right]}{\left[U\right]} = \dfrac{\left[k\right]\left[t\right]}{\left[x\right]\left[\dfrac{E}{V}\right]} = \dfrac{\left[\dfrac{E}{t}\right]\left[t\right]}{\left[x\right]\left[\dfrac{E}{V}\right]}$

$⇒ \left[\beta\right] = \dfrac{\left[{L}^{3}\right]}{\left[L\right]} = \left[{M}^{0}{L}^{2}{T}^{0}\right]$

questions.q: Potential energy as a function of $r$ is given by $U = \dfrac{A}{{r}^{10}} - \dfrac{B}{{r}^{5}}$, where $r$ is the interatomic distance, $A$ and $B$ are positive constants. The equilibrium distance between the two atoms will be :
questions.solution:
Given $U = \dfrac{A}{{r}^{10}} - \dfrac{B}{{r}^{5}}$.

Now, for equilibrium, $\dfrac{d U}{d r} = 0$.

So, differentiating the given equation,

$\dfrac{- 10A}{{r}^{11}} + \dfrac{5B}{{r}^{6}} = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{10A}{{r}^{11}} = \dfrac{5B}{{r}^{6}} ⇒ {r}^{5} = \dfrac{2A}{B} ⇒ r = \left(\dfrac{2A}{B}\right)\dfrac{1}{5}$

questions.q: A body of mass $0 . 5kg$ travels on straight line path with velocity $v = \left(3{x}^{2} + 4\right)m{s}^{- 1}$. The net work done by the force during its displacement from $x = 0$ to $x = 2m$ is
questions.solution:
Given: $v = 3{x}^{2} + 4$

Initial and final velocities are ${v}_{i} = 3{\left(0\right)}^{2} + 4 = 4m{s}^{- 1}$

and ${v}_{f} = 3{\left(2\right)}^{2} + 4 = 16m{s}^{- 1}$

From work-energy theorem,

$⇒ \DeltaKE = \dfrac{1}{2}m\left({v}_{f}^{2} - {v}_{i}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ \DeltaKE = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2}\left({16}^{2} - {4}^{2}\right)$

$⇒ \DeltaKE = W = 60J$
